prize_parts.citation: for foundational contributions to the theory of nominal rigidities, staggered price and contract setting, and policy rules that underpin the modern New Keynesian framework for monetary policy

statement.case_for: I keep B014 first. Time-dependent staggered pricing (Calvo), staggered contracts with an interest-rate policy rule (Taylor), and the microfounded, welfare-based synthesis (Woodford) are separate and identifiable building blocks. Together they form the framework in which monetary policy is now analysed and conducted, so the scientific and practical reach is very large. The core ideas are 25 to 40 years old, so there is no maturity concern. The three named people correspond to three distinct, traceable intellectual steps (price-setting device, contract and rule, unified framework). That makes the attribution defensible even though the field is crowded. The case rests on the originality and durability of these building blocks, not on how many members currently rank the candidate highly.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Eight names are credited, and a three-person cap leaves out Galí, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets, who developed the estimated medium-scale model and the Phillips-curve and empirical strands. The framework's empirical performance after 2008 and in the post-2021 inflation episode is also contested. A prize that is read as endorsing the baseline model's empirical adequacy, rather than recognising its conceptual and institutional role, could be criticised.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B014 second and calls it the hardest candidate on which to draw a defensible line. He cites attribution spread over eight names, possible reluctance to honour macro-policy frameworks again, and the debate over the baseline model after the post-2020 inflation. He ranks empirical optimal taxation (B007) first.
responses.response: I agree the line is hard, and it is the main weakness of B014. I would still separate the question of who originated a building block from who refined or estimated it. Calvo, Taylor and Woodford each introduced a distinct, citable component that others then took up, and that is a different situation from a diffuse craft contribution. On inflation, I would credit the framework's conceptual and institutional role, and the citation I propose says so. It does not claim the baseline model forecasts well. Weak performance in one episode does not undo the contribution, though it should shape the citation wording. I also do not see B007 as clearly stronger on attribution. Credit there is spread across Saez, Slemrod and Chetty, with Feldstein's early role ineligible and Chetty's work overlapping other candidates.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B014 sixth and proposes Woodford, Galí and Gertler as the most synthetic contributors to the modern framework. He flags the credit-allocation problem across at least eight names, mixed empirical evidence on the Phillips curve, and the risk that earlier macro prizes already cover nearby ground.
responses.response: The Woodford, Galí, Gertler trio is a reasonable alternative. It credits the New Keynesian Phillips curve and the policy-analysis synthesis. But it leaves out the staggered-pricing device and the policy rule, which are the earliest and most widely used pieces, and Galí and Gertler's work builds on them. I prefer to credit the originators of the components first and treat the later synthesis as the second layer. I accept that this is a judgement and not a fact. I take his point about the Phillips curve seriously. Its empirical status is mixed, which argues for a citation centred on nominal rigidities and policy rules rather than on any specific curve. I do not think earlier macro prizes (rational expectations, DSGE methodology, time-series methods) cover this ground. They address different contributions.

responses.point: Teorell ranks Kiyotaki-Moore (B042) first. He argues the 1997 credit-cycles paper gives a clean two-person attribution and a foundational macro-finance mechanism. He accepts that overlap with the 2022 banking-crisis prize and weaker direct empirical validation are real concerns.
responses.response: I agree B042 has the cleaner attribution, and I rank it second for that reason. My difference with Teorell is breadth of consequence, not quality. B014 is used daily in policy institutions, and the collateral-constraint mechanism is more theoretical and less directly tested. The overlap with the 2022 prize is the point that most worries me about B042. I read the 2022 prize as covering banking and financial-crisis theory and the Great Depression evidence, so it is complementary rather than redundant. That judgement is uncertain, which is why I keep B042 as my first alternative and not a co-equal second part. Adding it as a second part would also exceed the three-person limit with my preferred B014 trio.

uncertainties: Whether Calvo, Taylor and Woodford is the right three. Galí, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum or Smets could reasonably replace one of them, and the committee may prefer the estimated medium-scale DSGE strand.
How much weight the committee gives the post-2008 and post-2021 inflation critiques of the framework, and whether they should shape the citation wording.
Whether the Kiyotaki-Moore overlap with the 2022 prize is better read as complementary or redundant. I cannot resolve this from the supplied materials.

Whether the China-shock evidence in B032 is stable enough in magnitude and persistence, and how its credit is split between the task framework and the trade-shock work, given that Acemoglu and Restrepo are not on the ballot.
My own judgements rest on my own reading and the supplied profiles. I have not independently verified citations, dates or prior prizes.
statement.conflict_note: I am a frequent co-author with Per Krusell (secretary) and a co-author with John Hassler (chair). I am an IIES colleague of both, and both rank B014 highly. I also have a long-running collaboration with Peter Klenow (relevant to B030, which is not in my configuration) and work in heterogeneous-agent macro (B012, not shortlisted). None of the five people credited in my preferred or alternative B014 and B042 parts (Calvo, Taylor, Woodford, Kiyotaki, Moore) is a documented co-author of mine, though I work in the same broad field. I disclose these connections without adjudicating them.
